claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text with supporting citations to prior work.

claims.claim: VOT is a critical cue that listeners use to distinguish voiced from voiceless stop consonants in English.
claims.source: For example, voice-onset time (VOT), defined as the interval between a stop consonant's release and the onset of vocal fold vibration (acoustically, the burst and the voicing), is a critical cue that listeners use to distinguish voiced (e.g., /b/, /d/, /g/) from voiceless (e.g., /p/, /t/, /k/) stop consonants in English (Liberman et al., 1958; Lisker and Abramson, 1964).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to foundational work on VOT perception.

claims.claim: When the burst and voicing are roughly coincident (short VOT; ~0 ms), listeners perceive a bilabial stop as a /b/.
claims.source: When the burst and voicing are roughly coincident (short VOT; ~0 ms), listeners perceive a bilabial stop as a /b/, but when voicing follows the burst after a temporal gap (long VOT; ~50 ms), listeners hear a /p/.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and reflects established knowledge about VOT perception.

claims.claim: When voicing follows the burst after a temporal gap (long VOT; ~50 ms), listeners hear a /p/.
claims.source: When the burst and voicing are roughly coincident (short VOT; ~0 ms), listeners perceive a bilabial stop as a /b/, but when voicing follows the burst after a temporal gap (long VOT; ~50 ms), listeners hear a /p/.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and reflects established knowledge about VOT perception.

claims.claim: Information about a speech sound's identity is encoded in the amplitude of neural activity at phonetically-tuned cortical sites in the superior temporal gyrus (STG).
claims.source: Recent evidence from human electrocorticography (ECoG) has shown that information about a speech sound's identity is encoded in the amplitude of neural activity at phonetically-tuned cortical sites in the superior temporal gyrus (STG) (Mesgarani et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior ECoG work.

claims.claim: Distinct neural populations in STG respond selectively to different classes of phonemes that share certain spectral cues.
claims.source: Distinct neural populations in this region respond selectively to different classes of phonemes that share certain spectral cues, such as the burst associated with stop consonants or the characteristic formant structure of vowels produced with specific vocal tract configurations.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and reflects prior findings about phonetic selectivity in STG.

claims.claim: The exact VOT of a given utterance of a /b/ or a /p/ will vary considerably depending on numerous factors such as speech rate, phonetic context, and speaker accent.
claims.source: In addition to distinguishing phonetic categories, the exact VOT of a given utterance of a /b/ or a /p/ will vary considerably depending on numerous factors such as speech rate, phonetic context, and speaker accent (Miller et al., 1986; Kessinger and Blumstein, 1997; Klatt, 1975; Lisker and Abramson, 1967; Allen et al., 2003; Flege and Eefting, 1986; Fox et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting sources of VOT variability.

claims.claim: Sensitivity to fine-grained sub-phonetic detail is crucial for robust speech perception, allowing listeners to flexibly adapt and to integrate multiple cues to phonetic identity online in noisy, unstable environments.
claims.source: Although only categorical phonetic identity (e.g., whether a particular VOT is more consistent with a /b/ or a /p/) is strictly necessary for understanding meaning, sensitivity to fine-grained sub-phonetic detail (e.g., whether a particular /p/ was pronounced with a 40 ms vs. a 50 ms VOT) is also crucial for robust speech perception, allowing listeners to flexibly adapt and to integrate multiple cues to phonetic identity online in noisy, unstable environments (Miller and Volaitis, 1989; Clayards et al., 2008; Kleinschmidt and Jaeger, 2015; McMurray and Jongman, 2011; Toscano and McMurray, 2010; Fox and Blumstein, 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to work on perceptual adaptation and cue integration.

claims.claim: Listeners are sensitive to sub-phonetic detail in speech sounds.
claims.source: However, the neurophysiological mechanisms that support listeners' sensitivity (Kuhl, 1991; Carney, 1977; Pisoni and Tash, 1974; Massaro and Cohen, 1983; Andruski et al., 1994; McMurray et al., 2002; Schouten et al., 2003) to such detailed speech representations are not known.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting behavioral sensitivity to sub-phonetic detail.

claims.claim: Participants listened to and categorized speech sounds from a digitally synthesized continuum of consonant-vowel syllables that differed linearly only in their voice-onset time (VOT) from /ba/ (0 ms VOT) to /pa/ (50 ms VOT).
claims.source: Participants listened to and categorized speech sounds from a digitally synthesized continuum of consonant-vowel syllables that differed linearly only in their voice-onset time (VOT) from /ba/ (0 ms VOT) to /pa/ (50 ms VOT).
claims.evidence: The claim describes the experimental stimuli used in the study.

claims.claim: The six-step VOT continuum was constructed by manipulating only the relative timing of the spectral burst and the onset of voicing while holding all other acoustic properties of the stimuli constant.
claims.source: This six-step continuum was constructed by manipulating only the relative timing of the spectral burst and the onset of voicing while holding all other acoustic properties of the stimuli constant (Figure 1A/B; see Materials and methods) (Klatt, 1980).
claims.evidence: The claim describes the stimulus construction method and references Figure 1A/B showing the stimuli.

claims.claim: Stimuli with longer VOTs were more often labeled as /pa/.
claims.source: Analysis of participants' identification behavior confirmed that stimuli with longer VOTs were more often labeled as /pa/ (mixed effects logistic regression: βVOT = 0.19, t = 17.78, p=5.6*10−63; data for example participant in Figure 1C; data for all participants in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and references to figures showing the results.

claims.claim: Listeners' perception of the linear VOT continuum was sharply non-linear, a behavioral hallmark of categorical perception.
claims.source: Moreover, and consistent with past work, listeners' perception of the linear VOT continuum was sharply non-linear, a behavioral hallmark of categorical perception (Liberman et al., 1957; Liberman et al., 1961; Kronrod et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data and citations to prior work on categorical perception.

claims.claim: A psychophysical category boundary between 20 ms and 30 ms divided the continuum into stimuli most often perceived as voiced (/b/: 0 ms, 10 ms, 20 ms VOTs) or as voiceless (/p/: 30 ms, 40 ms, 50 ms VOTs).
claims.source: A psychophysical category boundary between 20 ms and 30 ms divided the continuum into stimuli most often perceived as voiced (/b/: 0 ms, 10 ms, 20 ms VOTs) or as voiceless (/p/: 30 ms, 40 ms, 50 ms VOTs).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of behavioral identification data.

claims.claim: 49 VOT-sensitive sites were found, primarily located over the lateral mid-to-posterior STG, bilaterally.
claims.source: Across all participants, we found 49 VOT-sensitive sites, primarily located over the lateral mid-to-posterior STG, bilaterally.
claims.evidence: The claim reports the number and location of VOT-sensitive electrodes identified in the study.

claims.claim: Peak response amplitude at VOT-sensitive electrodes reliably discriminated between voicing categories, exhibiting stronger responses to either voiced (/b/; VOT = 0–20 ms; n = 33) or voiceless (/p/; VOT = 30–50 ms; n = 16) stimuli.
claims.source: Peak response amplitude at these VOT-sensitive electrodes reliably discriminated between voicing categories, exhibiting stronger responses to either voiced (/b/; VOT = 0–20 ms; n = 33) or voiceless (/p/; VOT = 30–50 ms; n = 16) stimuli (Figure 1D; locations of all sites shown in Figures 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by neural data analysis and references to figures showing electrode locations and selectivity.

claims.claim: Within individual participants, electrodes spaced only 4 mm apart showed strong preferences for different voicing categories.
claims.source: We observed that, within individual participants, electrodes spaced only 4 mm apart showed strong preferences for different voicing categories, and we did not observe any clear overall regional or hemispheric patterns in the prevalence or selectivity patterns of VOT-sensitive electrodes (see Materials and methods for additional information).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on spatial analysis of electrode selectivity patterns.

claims.claim: Robust category selectivity in voiceless-selective (V-) and voiced-selective (V+) neural populations emerged as early as 50–150 ms post-stimulus onset and often lasted for several hundred milliseconds.
claims.source: Robust category selectivity in voiceless-selective (V-) and voiced-selective (V+) neural populations emerged as early as 50–150 ms post-stimulus onset and often lasted for several hundred milliseconds (example electrodes in Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim describes the temporal dynamics of category selectivity and references Figure 1E showing example time courses.

claims.claim: Voicing category selectivity was reliable whether a trial's voicing category was defined based on the psychophysically-determined category boundary or based on the actual behavioral response recorded for each trial.
claims.source: Across all VOT-sensitive electrodes, voicing category selectivity was reliable whether a trial's voicing category was defined based on the psychophysically-determined category boundary (0–20 ms vs. 30–50 ms VOTs; V- electrodes: z = 3.52, p=4.4×10−4; V+ electrodes: z = −5.01, p=5.4×10−7; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests) or based on the actual behavioral response recorded for each trial (V- electrodes: p=4.9×10−4; V+ electrodes: p=6.1×10−5; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical tests on neural data using two different definitions of voicing category.

claims.claim: Spatially distinct neural populations in auditory cortex are tuned to speech sound categories defined by a temporal cue.
claims.source: These results show that spatially distinct neural populations in auditory cortex are tuned to speech sound categories defined by a temporal cue.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the neural data showing category-selective responses.

claims.claim: If individual neural populations only responded to spectral features, we would not have observed overall amplitude differences in their responses to /b/ versus /p/ categories.
claims.source: Critically, if individual neural populations only responded to spectral features (e.g., to the burst or to the onset of voicing), we would not have observed overall amplitude differences in their responses to /b/ versus /p/ categories.
claims.evidence: The claim is a logical inference about what the results imply regarding temporal integration.

claims.claim: Across participants, classification accuracy for voicing category was significantly better than chance.
claims.source: We found that, across participants, classification accuracy was significantly better than chance (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p=0.016; Figure 1F, leftmost box plot), demonstrating that spatially and temporally distributed population neural activity during the peak response contains information that allows for decoding of a temporally-cued phonetic distinction in speech.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of classifier performance and references Figure 1F showing the results.

claims.claim: Spatially and temporally distributed population neural activity during the peak response contains information that allows for decoding of a temporally-cued phonetic distinction in speech.
claims.source: We found that, across participants, classification accuracy was significantly better than chance (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p=0.016; Figure 1F, leftmost box plot), demonstrating that spatially and temporally distributed population neural activity during the peak response contains information that allows for decoding of a temporally-cued phonetic distinction in speech.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the successful classification of voicing category from neural data.

claims.claim: When the classifiers had access to amplitude information but not timing information during the peak response, performance was significantly better than chance.
claims.source: Across participants, we found that, when the classifiers had access to amplitude information but not timing information (+Amplitude/-Timing) during the peak response, performance was significantly better than chance (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p=0.016; Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of classifier performance with corrupted timing information.

claims.claim: Classification accuracy with amplitude information alone was statistically comparable to the model that had access to both amplitude and timing information.
claims.source: Furthermore, despite the profound corruption of temporal information in the neural responses, classification accuracy was statistically comparable to the model that had access to both amplitude and timing information (+Amplitude/+Timing; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p=0.69; Figure 1F), suggesting that amplitude information alone is sufficient for classifying a trial's voicing category.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of classifier performance under different conditions.

claims.claim: Amplitude information alone is sufficient for classifying a trial's voicing category.
claims.source: Furthermore, despite the profound corruption of temporal information in the neural responses, classification accuracy was statistically comparable to the model that had access to both amplitude and timing information (+Amplitude/+Timing; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p=0.69; Figure 1F), suggesting that amplitude information alone is sufficient for classifying a trial's voicing category.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the classifier performance results.

claims.claim: When amplitude information was corrupted and only temporal patterns in the peak response window were reliable, classifier performance was not different from chance.
claims.source: In contrast, when amplitude information was corrupted and only temporal patterns in the peak response window were reliable (-Amplitude/+Timing), classifier performance was not different from chance (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p=0.69; Figure 1F) and was worse for every participant compared to the model with both types of information (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p=0.016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of classifier performance with corrupted amplitude information.

claims.claim: Preserving timing information alone had no effect on classification performance compared to the most impoverished model where both amplitude and timing information were corrupted.
claims.source: Finally, we compared the model with only timing information to a model where both amplitude and timing information during the peak window were corrupted (-Amplitude/-Timing). We found that preserving timing information alone had no effect on classification performance compared to the most impoverished model (-Amplitude/-Timing; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p=0.58; Figure 1F), which also failed to perform better than chance (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p=0.94; Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of classifier performance under different conditions.

claims.claim: Localized peak high-gamma response amplitude spatially encodes voicing of single trials in STG, analogous to other spectrally-cued phonetic features.
claims.source: Together, these results constitute evidence for a spatial/amplitude code for speech categories that differ in a temporal cue. Thus, localized peak high-gamma response amplitude spatially encodes voicing of single trials in STG, analogous to other spectrally-cued phonetic features (Mesgarani et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the classifier results and is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Across all V- and V+ electrodes, peak high-gamma response amplitude encoded stimulus VOT within the preferred category but not the non-preferred category.
claims.source: Across all V- and V+ electrodes, peak high-gamma response amplitude encoded stimulus VOT within the preferred category (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = 6.02, p=1.7×10−9), but not the non-preferred category (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = 1.31, p=0.19).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of within-category VOT encoding.

claims.claim: V- electrodes encoded sub-phonetic VOT more robustly within the voiceless category than within the voiced category.
claims.source: While V- electrodes encoded sub-phonetic VOT more robustly within the voiceless category than within the voiced category (Figure 2D, left; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = 3.00, p=2.7×10−3), the opposite pattern emerged for V+ electrodes, which encoded sub-phonetic VOT more robustly within the voiced category than within the voiceless category (Figure 2D, right; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = 3.78, p=1.6×10−4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and references Figure 2D showing the encoding patterns.

claims.claim: V+ electrodes encoded sub-phonetic VOT more robustly within the voiced category than within the voiceless category.
claims.source: While V- electrodes encoded sub-phonetic VOT more robustly within the voiceless category than within the voiced category (Figure 2D, left; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = 3.00, p=2.7×10−3), the opposite pattern emerged for V+ electrodes, which encoded sub-phonetic VOT more robustly within the voiced category than within the voiceless category (Figure 2D, right; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = 3.78, p=1.6×10−4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and references Figure 2D showing the encoding patterns.

claims.claim: VOT encoding in human STG is not purely categorical.
claims.source: Together, these analyses revealed two key results: (1) VOT encoding in human STG is not purely categorical, but also (2) the relationship between response amplitude and VOT is not linear across the entire continuum (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the within-category encoding analysis.

claims.claim: The relationship between response amplitude and VOT is not linear across the entire continuum.
claims.source: Together, these analyses revealed two key results: (1) VOT encoding in human STG is not purely categorical, but also (2) the relationship between response amplitude and VOT is not linear across the entire continuum (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the within-category encoding analysis and references Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Individual neural populations in human auditory cortex encode information about both the category identity of a speech sound and its more fine-grained acoustic properties, or its category goodness.
claims.source: These results suggest that, even at the level of STG, the brain maintains information about the specific, sub-phonetic details of individual speech sounds. The asymmetrical pattern of within-category encoding suggests that individual neural populations in human auditory cortex encode information about both the category identity of a speech sound and its more fine-grained acoustic properties, or its category goodness (Kuhl, 1991; Blumstein et al., 2005; Myers, 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the asymmetric within-category encoding pattern and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: A temporal cue that distinguishes speech sounds is represented by a spatial/amplitude code in human STG.
claims.source: Thus far, we have demonstrated that a temporal cue that distinguishes speech sounds is represented by a spatial/amplitude code (Ferster and Spruston, 1995; Shadlen and Newsome, 1994) in human STG.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary of the main finding and is supported by citations to prior work on spatial/amplitude coding.

claims.claim: The entire neural network model is comprised of just five localist units: a burst detector, a voicing detector, a gap detector (Gap), a coincidence detector (Coinc), and an inhibitory unit.
claims.source: The entire model is comprised of just five localist units: a burst detector, a voicing detector, a gap detector (Gap), a coincidence detector (Coinc), and an inhibitory unit.
claims.evidence: The claim describes the architecture of the computational model.

claims.claim: There are striking qualitative similarities between Gap simulated outputs and the real neural responses of V- electrodes.
claims.source: The simulated responses of Gap and Coinc to VOTs of 0–50 ms are shown in Figure 2F/G. We observed striking qualitative similarities between Gap simulated outputs (Figure 2F) and the real neural responses of V- electrodes (Figure 2B), and between Coinc outputs (Figure 2G) and the V+ electrodes (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on comparison of model simulations to neural data shown in figures.

claims.claim: There are striking qualitative similarities between Coinc outputs and the V+ electrodes.
claims.source: The simulated responses of Gap and Coinc to VOTs of 0–50 ms are shown in Figure 2F/G. We observed striking qualitative similarities between Gap simulated outputs (Figure 2F) and the real neural responses of V- electrodes (Figure 2B), and between Coinc outputs (Figure 2G) and the V+ electrodes (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on comparison of model simulations to neural data shown in figures.

claims.claim: Spatial encoding of temporal cues (gaps vs. coincidences) can arise naturally within a simple, biologically-inspired neural network.
claims.source: By design, voicing category is clearly distinguished in both Gap and Coinc, with Gap responding more strongly to longer (voiceless) VOTs (30–50 ms), and Coinc responding more strongly to shorter (voiced) VOTs (0–20 ms). This demonstrates that spatial encoding of temporal cues (gaps vs. coincidences) can arise naturally within a simple, biologically-inspired neural network (Buonomano and Merzenich, 1995; Gao and Wehr, 2015; Eggermont, 2000; Carr, 1993; Konishi, 2003; Rauschecker, 2014; Rauschecker, 1998).
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the model simulations and is supported by citations to prior work on temporal processing.

claims.claim: Both Gap and Coinc detector units exhibit sensitivity to within-category VOT distinctions.
claims.source: Perhaps more surprisingly, we also found that both Gap and Coinc detector units exhibit sensitivity to within-category VOT distinctions (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of model outputs shown in Figure 2H.

claims.claim: V- electrodes and Gap units are only sensitive to differences among long (voiceless) VOTs.
claims.source: These partially graded activations mirror the pattern observed in the neural data (Figure 2D), where V- electrodes and Gap units are only sensitive to differences among long (voiceless) VOTs, and V+ electrodes and Coinc units are only sensitive to differences among short (voiced) VOTs.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on comparison of model outputs to neural data patterns.

claims.claim: V+ electrodes and Coinc units are only sensitive to differences among short (voiced) VOTs.
claims.source: These partially graded activations mirror the pattern observed in the neural data (Figure 2D), where V- electrodes and Gap units are only sensitive to differences among long (voiceless) VOTs, and V+ electrodes and Coinc units are only sensitive to differences among short (voiced) VOTs.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on comparison of model outputs to neural data patterns.

claims.claim: The timing of the evoked neural responses (relative to burst onset) appeared to depend on stimulus VOT in V+ electrodes and in the coincidence detector (Coinc) unit, but not in V- electrodes or in the gap detector (Gap) unit.
claims.source: However, in comparing the real and simulated neural data (Figure 2), we also observed a qualitative resemblance with respect to the onset latencies of evoked responses. Specifically, the timing of the evoked neural responses (relative to burst onset) appeared to depend on stimulus VOT in V+ electrodes and in the coincidence detector (Coinc) unit (Figure 2C/G), but not in V- electrodes or in the gap detector (Gap) unit (Figure 2B/F).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on visual comparison of neural data and model simulations shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Response onset latency was strongly associated with VOT for V+, but not V-, electrodes.
claims.source: We found that response onset latency was strongly associated with VOT for V+, but not V-, electrodes (Wilcoxon signed-rank tests: V+, p=1.6×10−6; V-, p=0.57), and this difference between the two electrode types was highly reliable (Mann-Whitney rank-sum test: p=1.7×10−5) (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of onset latency data and references Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The same well-established physiological mechanisms that give rise to peak amplitude encoding of temporally-cued voicing categories also predict the early temporal dynamics observed in real neural data.
claims.source: Thus, the same well-established physiological mechanisms that give rise to peak amplitude encoding of temporally-cued voicing categories also predict the early temporal dynamics we observe in real neural data.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the model's ability to capture both amplitude and temporal dynamics.

claims.claim: Both sub-phonetic and phonetic category-level information are carried by the onset latency of V+ electrodes.
claims.source: Finally, Figure 3 shows that, unlike during the peak response window (150–250 ms after stimulus onset; Figure 1F), temporal information does encode VOT during an earlier window around the neural response onset in some neural populations. Indeed, both sub-phonetic and phonetic category-level information are carried by the onset latency of V+ electrodes, with evoked responses arising later at these sites for stimuli with progressively longer VOTs.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of onset latency data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Both the amplitude encoding patterns during the peak window and the temporal encoding patterns during the earlier onset window are captured by the same canonical neurophysiological mechanisms.
claims.source: Critically, the modeling results indicate that both the amplitude encoding patterns during the peak window and the temporal encoding patterns during the earlier onset window are captured by the same canonical neurophysiological mechanisms.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the model's ability to capture multiple aspects of the neural data.

claims.claim: Discrete neural populations located primarily on the bilateral posterior and middle STG respond preferentially to either voiced sounds or voiceless sounds.
claims.source: Using direct intracranial recordings, we found discrete neural populations located primarily on the bilateral posterior and middle STG that respond preferentially to either voiced sounds, where the onset of voicing is coincident with the burst or follows it after a short lag (20 ms or less), or voiceless sounds, where the onset of voicing follows the burst after a temporal gap of at least 30–50 ms.
claims.evidence: The claim summarizes the main finding about neural population selectivity.

claims.claim: The cortical representation of both spectral and temporal cues in speech follow a common spatial coding scheme.
claims.source: The present results extend these earlier findings in a critical way, suggesting that the cortical representation of both spectral and temporal cues in speech follow a common spatial coding scheme.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the current results in the context of prior work.

claims.claim: The digitally synthesized VOT stimuli were tightly controlled to vary only in the relative timing of two invariant spectral cues (burst and voicing).
claims.source: This result is also consistent with prior reports that neural response amplitude depends on VOT (Mesgarani et al., 2014), but such results have often involved natural speech stimuli where voicing categories varied along many other spectral acoustic dimensions besides the temporal cue (Lisker, 1986; Soli, 1983; Stevens and Klatt, 1974; Summerfield and Haggard, 1977). Here, the digitally synthesized VOT stimuli were tightly controlled to vary only in the relative timing of two invariant spectral cues (burst and voicing), thereby demonstrating that this temporal speech cue is encoded in the peak high-gamma response amplitude of spatially distinct neural populations in human STG.
claims.evidence: The claim describes the stimulus control used in the study and is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: This temporal speech cue is encoded in the peak high-gamma response amplitude of spatially distinct neural populations in human STG.
claims.source: Here, the digitally synthesized VOT stimuli were tightly controlled to vary only in the relative timing of two invariant spectral cues (burst and voicing), thereby demonstrating that this temporal speech cue is encoded in the peak high-gamma response amplitude of spatially distinct neural populations in human STG.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the neural data with controlled stimuli.

claims.claim: Temporal and amplitude codes for VOT are not mutually exclusive.
claims.source: Our examination of the timing and amplitude of three peaks in the auditory evoked local field potentials of VOT-sensitive electrodes confirmed that such patterns do appear in some electrodes (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4), clearly demonstrating that temporal and amplitude codes for VOT are not mutually exclusive (see also temporal encoding patterns in onset latencies of V+ electrodes; Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of local field potential data shown in supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The amplitude of the peak high-gamma (and, in many cases, of the LFP) response emerged as a robust representation of voicing category and of VOT.
claims.source: However, as with spectrally-defined phonetic contrasts (e.g., plosive vs. fricative; Mesgarani et al., 2014), it clear that the amplitude of the peak high-gamma (and, in many cases, of the LFP) response emerged as a robust representation of voicing category and of VOT.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the neural data analysis and is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The fact that we found cortical sites in every participant that exhibited robust category-dependent differences in their peak response amplitude rules out the possibility that at least these neural populations are merely responding to spectral cues in the burst or voicing alone.
claims.source: However, the fact that we found cortical sites in every participant that exhibited robust category-dependent differences in their peak response amplitude rules out the possibility that at least these neural populations are merely responding to spectral cues in the burst or voicing alone.
claims.evidence: The claim is a logical inference drawn from the pattern of neural responses.

claims.claim: Corrupting peak amplitude information had a devastating effect on the decoding of voicing category, while corrupting the fine temporal patterns had no measurable impact on classifier performance.
claims.source: Notably, if either (or both) of these models – a local or ensemble temporal code – was primarily responsible for the neural representation of VOT in the high-gamma range, then the selective corruption of temporal information in a classifier (Figure 1F) should have reduced neural decoding of voicing category to chance levels, while corrupting peak amplitude information should have had little or no effect. We found the opposite pattern of results: corrupting peak amplitude information had a devastating effect on the decoding of voicing category, while corrupting the fine temporal patterns that could have discriminated between voicing categories had no measurable impact on classifier performance.
claims.evidence: The claim summarizes the classifier results and their implications.

claims.claim: Our work does not rule out the possibility that local or ensemble temporal codes may also play a role in the cortical representation of VOT.
claims.source: To be clear, our work does not rule out the possibility that local or ensemble temporal codes may also play a role in the cortical representation of VOT.
claims.evidence: The claim acknowledges limitations of the study's conclusions.

claims.claim: Spatially-localized peak neural response amplitude is a robust code for VOT.
claims.source: However, it does highlight spatially-localized peak neural response amplitude as a robust code for VOT.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the classifier results.

claims.claim: There is evidence for a shared representation of both spectrally- and temporally-cued phonetic features by high-gamma responses in the human superior temporal lobe.
claims.source: Thus, in contrast to prior work theorizing parallel, but fundamentally different, coding schemes for spectrally- and temporally-cued phonetic features (Steinschneider et al., 1999; Steinschneider et al., 2013), we demonstrate evidence for a shared representation of both by high-gamma responses in the human superior temporal lobe.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the results and contrasts with prior theories, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The model highlights one parsimonious approach by which selectivity for either temporal gaps or coincidences could be implemented by biologically-inspired neurophysiological microcircuits.
claims.source: Our model highlights one parsimonious approach by which selectivity for either temporal gaps or coincidences could be implemented by biologically-inspired neurophysiological microcircuits (Buonomano and Merzenich, 1995; Gao and Wehr, 2015; Eggermont, 2000; Carr, 1993; Konishi, 2003; Rauschecker, 2014; Rauschecker, 1998).
claims.evidence: The claim describes the contribution of the computational model and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: Gap and coincidence detector units responded to simulated voiced (/b/) and voiceless (/p/) stimuli with different response amplitudes.
claims.source: We found that, just like in the neural data, gap and coincidence detector units responded to simulated voiced (/b/) and voiceless (/p/) stimuli with different response amplitudes.
claims.evidence: The claim describes the model's behavior in simulations.

claims.claim: We need not invoke any specialized temporal code to account for the representation of temporally cued phonetic features.
claims.source: As such, we need not invoke any specialized temporal code to account for the representation of temporally cued phonetic features.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the model's ability to capture the neural data.

claims.claim: Our results provide evidence implicating a common neural coding scheme in the neural representation of behaviorally relevant speech features, whether they are embedded within the instantaneous spectrum or the fine temporal structure of the speech signal.
claims.source: Rather, our results provide evidence implicating a common neural coding scheme in the neural representation of behaviorally relevant speech features, whether they are embedded within the instantaneous spectrum or the fine temporal structure of the speech signal.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the overall results of the study.

claims.claim: Different neural populations encode pitch and key properties of the speech envelope such as onsets and auditory edges.
claims.source: Recent ECoG evidence suggests an even more expansive view of the fundamental role of spatial coding in cortical speech representation (Yi et al., 2019) in which different neural populations also encode pitch (Tang et al., 2017) and key properties of the speech envelope such as onsets and auditory edges (Hamilton et al., 2018; Oganian and Chang, 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent ECoG studies.

claims.claim: Although the neural network was only designed to discriminate between categories, graded amplitude differences in response to different VOTs emerged naturally from the same computational properties.
claims.source: Crucially, although the neural network was only designed to discriminate between categories (i.e., gaps vs. coincidences), we also observed graded amplitude differences in response to different VOTs (Figure 2H), but only in an electrode's preferred category. These within-category patterns emerged naturally from the same computational properties that allowed the network to capture basic between-category encoding: (1) the relative responsiveness of each temporal integrator unit (Gap, Coinc) to its various inputs (burst, voicing, and inhibition); (2) the time-dependent properties inherent to neuronal activation dynamics (e.g., decay of postsynaptic potentials towards a unit's resting activation level); and (3) the nonlinear transformation of postsynaptic inputs into response outputs (rectified linear activation function controlled by a unit's propagation threshold).
claims.evidence: The claim describes an emergent property of the model and the mechanisms responsible.

claims.claim: This asymmetric within-category encoding scheme closely resembled the pattern observed in real neurophysiological data.
claims.source: This asymmetric within-category encoding scheme closely resembled the pattern observed in real neurophysiological data, where peak response amplitude to VOTs within the same voicing category only differed within a neural population's preferred category (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on comparison of model outputs to neural data.

claims.claim: Human nonprimary auditory cortex maintains a robust, graded representation of VOT that includes the sub-phonetic details about how a particular speech token was pronounced.
claims.source: This result clearly demonstrates that human nonprimary auditory cortex maintains a robust, graded representation of VOT that includes the sub-phonetic details about how a particular speech token was pronounced (Blumstein et al., 2005; Toscano et al., 2010; Toscano et al., 2018; Frye et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the within-category encoding results and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: Fine-grained acoustic detail has demonstrable effects on listeners' behavior.
claims.source: Even though sub-phonetic information is not strictly necessary for mapping sound to meaning in stable, noise-free listening environments, this fine-grained acoustic detail has demonstrable effects on listeners' behavior (Kuhl, 1991; Carney, 1977; Pisoni and Tash, 1974; Massaro and Cohen, 1983; Andruski et al., 1994; McMurray et al., 2002; Schouten et al., 2003), and modern theories of speech perception agree that perceptual learning (e.g., adaptation to accented speakers) and robust cue integration would be impossible if the perception of speech sounds were strictly categorical (Miller and Volaitis, 1989; Clayards et al., 2008; Kleinschmidt and Jaeger, 2015; McMurray and Jongman, 2011; Toscano and McMurray, 2010; McClelland and Elman, 1986; Norris and McQueen, 2008; Norris et al., 2016; Magnuson et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to behavioral and theoretical work.

claims.claim: Modern theories of speech perception agree that perceptual learning and robust cue integration would be impossible if the perception of speech sounds were strictly categorical.
claims.source: Even though sub-phonetic information is not strictly necessary for mapping sound to meaning in stable, noise-free listening environments, this fine-grained acoustic detail has demonstrable effects on listeners' behavior (Kuhl, 1991; Carney, 1977; Pisoni and Tash, 1974; Massaro and Cohen, 1983; Andruski et al., 1994; McMurray et al., 2002; Schouten et al., 2003), and modern theories of speech perception agree that perceptual learning (e.g., adaptation to accented speakers) and robust cue integration would be impossible if the perception of speech sounds were strictly categorical (Miller and Volaitis, 1989; Clayards et al., 2008; Kleinschmidt and Jaeger, 2015; McMurray and Jongman, 2011; Toscano and McMurray, 2010; McClelland and Elman, 1986; Norris and McQueen, 2008; Norris et al., 2016; Magnuson et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to theoretical work on speech perception.

claims.claim: The same spatial/amplitude code that is implicated in the representation of phonetic information can also accommodate the representation of sub-phonetic information in the speech signal.
claims.source: Crucially, these data suggest that the same spatial/amplitude code that is implicated in the representation of phonetic information (from spectral or temporal cues) can also accommodate the representation of sub-phonetic information in the speech signal.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the within-category encoding results.

claims.claim: Response onset latencies of V- electrodes were time-locked to the burst.
claims.source: The onset latency results (Figure 3) established an entirely novel correspondence between the real and simulated results that extended beyond the peak response window. Response onset latencies of V- electrodes were time-locked to the burst (Figures 2B and 3), while responses of V+ electrodes were time-locked to voicing onset (Figures 2C and 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of onset latency data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Responses of V+ electrodes were time-locked to voicing onset.
claims.source: The onset latency results (Figure 3) established an entirely novel correspondence between the real and simulated results that extended beyond the peak response window. Response onset latencies of V- electrodes were time-locked to the burst (Figures 2B and 3), while responses of V+ electrodes were time-locked to voicing onset (Figures 2C and 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of onset latency data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The fact that the model's prediction is borne out in the neural data in STG is consistent with local temporal integration in STG.
claims.source: The model's gap and coincidence detectors (Gap, Coinc) are designed to directly simulate neural populations in the STG. Their inputs from the burst and voicing detectors are only spectrally processed, so in the model, the temporal onset latency dynamics (Figure 2F/G) first arise in Gap and Coinc. As such, the fact that the model's prediction is borne out in the neural data in STG (Figure 2B, C and 3) is consistent with local temporal integration in STG.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the correspondence between model predictions and neural data.

claims.claim: The model provides an explicit, mathematical account of multiple seemingly disparate observations about the neurophysiological data.
claims.source: Overall, the results of these model simulations illustrate how the same network properties that transform temporal cues into a spatial code are also able to naturally explain at least three additional patterns observed within category-selective neural populations: (1) the graded encoding of VOT within a population's preferred category; (2) the lack of graded encoding of VOT within a population's non-preferred category; and (3) the early temporal dynamics of neural responses, which depend on a population's category-selectivity. Thus, the model provides an explicit, mathematical account of multiple seemingly disparate observations about the neurophysiological data, all of which arise directly from a parsimonious implementation of gap- and coincidence-detection with well-established, theoretically-motivated neuronal circuits.
claims.evidence: The claim summarizes the explanatory power of the computational model.

claims.claim: The model predicted VOT-dependence in the latency of the peak response in both Gap and Coinc units, but we did not find evidence for these fine-grained patterns in the high-gamma data.
claims.source: While the model captured several notable features of the neural data (including some for which it was not explicitly designed), we observed at least one inconsistency between the simulated and real neural responses. The model predicted VOT-dependence in the latency of the peak response in both Gap and Coinc units (Figure 2F/G), but we did not find evidence for these fine-grained patterns in the high-gamma data (Figure 2B/C; see also lack of category-dependent temporal patterns during peak window: Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: The claim describes a discrepancy between model predictions and neural data.

claims.claim: VOT-sensitive neural populations were scattered throughout posterior and middle superior temporal gyrus with no discernible topographical map of selectivity or evidence for lateralized asymmetries.
claims.source: As with tuning for spectrally-cued phonetic features (Mesgarani et al., 2014; Hamilton et al., 2018) (e.g., plosives vs. fricatives), VOT-sensitive neural populations in the present study were scattered throughout posterior and middle superior temporal gyrus with no discernible topographical map of selectivity or evidence for lateralized asymmetries (Liégeois-Chauvel et al., 1999; Zatorre and Belin, 2001), although data limitations prevent us from ruling out this possibility entirely (for detailed results, see Material and methods).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on spatial analysis of electrode locations and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: There exist complex associations between VOT and the amplitude/temporal information carried in lower-frequency ranges.
claims.source: Indeed, it is clear from the exploratory analyses of auditory evoked local field potentials (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4) that there do exist complex associations between VOT and the amplitude/temporal information carried in lower-frequency ranges.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on exploratory analyses of local field potential data shown in supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Neural responses to different VOT tokens that are members of the same voicing category can only be considered truly categorical if the responses are indiscriminable.
claims.source: Finally, it is critical to distinguish our results from studies describing neural correlates of categorical speech perception, per se (e.g., Chang et al., 2010). Neural responses to different VOT tokens that are members of the same voicing category can only be considered truly categorical if the responses are indiscriminable (e.g., Liberman et al., 1957; Macmillan et al., 1977).
claims.evidence: The claim defines what would constitute truly categorical neural responses and is supported by citations.

claims.source: In our results, acoustically distinct members of the same phonetic category are distinguishable in neural populations that are selective for that voicing category (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the within-category encoding results shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The present results are best interpreted as elucidating neural mechanisms of category perception, but not necessarily categorical perception, of voiced vs. voiceless stop consonants.
claims.source: In light of this graded VOT representation, the present results are best interpreted as elucidating neural mechanisms of category perception, but not necessarily categorical perception, of voiced vs. voiceless stop consonants.
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the results in the context of categorical perception theory.

claims.claim: The model suggests that top-down effects may not be a necessary condition for explaining the observed non-linear encoding patterns.
claims.source: While limited coverage beyond the superior temporal lobe precludes us from ruling out the influence of top-down categorical perception (Lee et al., 2012; Myers et al., 2009; Evans and Davis, 2015) (possibly originating in frontal cortex; Sohoglu et al., 2012; Leonard et al., 2016; Cope et al., 2017; Park et al., 2015) on our results, it is notable that the model we present (which does not posit top-down effects) suggests that top-down effects may not be a necessary condition for explaining the observed non-linear encoding patterns (see also McClelland et al., 2006; McQueen et al., 2006; Norris et al., 2000; McClelland and Elman, 1986; Norris and McQueen, 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the model's ability to capture the data without top-down mechanisms, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Spatially-discrete neural populations in human auditory cortex are tuned to detect either gaps or coincidences between spectral cues.
claims.source: In conclusion, the present results show that spatially-discrete neural populations in human auditory cortex are tuned to detect either gaps or coincidences between spectral cues, and these sites simultaneously represent both phonetic and sub-phonetic information carried by VOT, a temporal speech cue found in almost all languages (Lisker and Abramson, 1964; Cho and Ladefoged, 1999).

results.result: Voice-onset time (VOT) is a critical temporal acoustic cue that listeners use to distinguish voiced from voiceless stop consonants in English, with short VOTs (~0 ms) perceived as /b/ and long VOTs (~50 ms) perceived as /p/.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 are well-established facts about VOT perception supported by foundational citations (Liberman et al., 1958; Lisker and Abramson, 1964). These claims provide essential background knowledge that is widely accepted in the field of speech perception.

results.result: Prior ECoG work has shown that speech sound identity is encoded in the amplitude of neural activity at phonetically-tuned cortical sites in STG, with distinct neural populations responding selectively to different classes of phonemes that share spectral cues.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6 accurately describe prior findings from Mesgarani et al. (2014) regarding spectral encoding of phonetic features in STG. These claims establish the context for the current study's investigation of temporal cue encoding.

results.result: VOT varies considerably depending on factors like speech rate, phonetic context, and speaker accent, and sensitivity to fine-grained sub-phonetic detail is crucial for robust speech perception, allowing listeners to flexibly adapt in noisy environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C9 are well-supported by multiple citations documenting VOT variability and the importance of sub-phonetic sensitivity for perceptual adaptation and cue integration. These claims establish the motivation for investigating sub-phonetic encoding.

results.result: Participants listened to a digitally synthesized VOT continuum from /ba/ to /pa/ that varied only in the relative timing of burst and voicing onset, and behavioral data showed that longer VOTs were more often labeled as /pa/ with a sharp non-linear perception characteristic of categorical perception, with a category boundary between 20-30 ms.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C14 describe the experimental stimuli and behavioral results. The stimulus control (C11) is well-documented, behavioral analysis (C12) shows significant effects (p=5.6×10⁻⁶³), and the categorical perception pattern (C13-C14) is consistent with prior work and supported by appropriate statistical analysis.

results.result: 49 VOT-sensitive sites were identified in bilateral mid-to-posterior STG that reliably discriminated between voicing categories based on peak response amplitude, with 33 voiced-selective and 16 voiceless-selective electrodes showing category selectivity as early as 50-150 ms post-stimulus onset, demonstrating that spatially distinct neural populations are tuned to speech sound categories defined by a temporal cue.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C21 describe the core neural finding of category-selective responses. The identification of VOT-sensitive sites is based on appropriate statistical methods (Spearman's ρ, p<0.05), category selectivity is confirmed with multiple statistical tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with highly significant p-values), and the spatial distribution is well-documented. The logical inference (C21) that these populations integrate temporal information is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Population-based classification of voicing category from neural activity during the peak response window (150-250 ms) was significantly better than chance, and this decoding was driven by amplitude information rather than temporal patterns, as corrupting amplitude information eliminated above-chance performance while corrupting timing information had no effect, demonstrating that localized peak high-gamma response amplitude spatially encodes voicing.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C29 describe the classifier analysis results. The above-chance classification (C22, p=0.016) is statistically significant. The selective corruption experiments (C24-C28) provide strong evidence that amplitude, not timing, drives classification during the peak window. The statistical comparisons are appropriate (Wilcoxon signed-rank tests), and the conclusion (C29) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Peak high-gamma response amplitude encoded stimulus VOT within each electrode's preferred category but not the non-preferred category, with V- electrodes showing graded responses to voiceless VOTs and V+ electrodes showing graded responses to voiced VOTs, demonstrating that VOT encoding in STG is not purely categorical and that individual neural populations encode both category identity and category goodness.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C35 describe within-category encoding patterns. The statistical analyses are appropriate (Wilcoxon signed-rank tests) with highly significant results (e.g., p=1.7×10⁻⁹ for preferred category encoding, p=2.7×10⁻³ and p=1.6×10⁻⁴ for asymmetric encoding). The conclusions about non-categorical encoding (C33-C34) and dual encoding of category identity and goodness (C35) are well-supported by the data and consistent with cited prior work.

results.result: A simple five-unit neural network model implementing gap and coincidence detection through leaky integrator dynamics captured the key patterns observed in neural data, including category selectivity, within-category encoding asymmetry, and the natural emergence of spatial encoding of temporal cues.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C43 describe the computational model and its ability to capture neural data patterns. The model architecture (C37) is clearly specified, and the qualitative similarities between model outputs and neural data (C38-C39) are demonstrated in figures. The model successfully captures both between-category (C40) and within-category (C41-C43) encoding patterns, providing mechanistic insight into how temporal cues can be transformed into spatial codes.

results.result: Response onset latency depended on VOT for V+ electrodes but not V- electrodes, with V+ electrodes showing time-locking to voicing onset, and this pattern was predicted by the same computational mechanisms in the model that explained peak amplitude encoding, demonstrating that both amplitude and temporal encoding patterns arise from the same neurophysiological mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C48 describe onset latency effects. The statistical analysis (C45) shows highly significant VOT-dependence for V+ electrodes (p=1.6×10⁻⁶) but not V- electrodes (p=0.57), with a significant difference between groups (p=1.7×10⁻⁵). The model predictions (C44, C46) match the neural data, and the conclusion (C48) that the same mechanisms explain both amplitude and temporal patterns is well-supported.

results.result: The study demonstrates that discrete neural populations in bilateral posterior and middle STG are tuned to detect gaps or coincidences between spectral cues, simultaneously representing both phonetic and sub-phonetic information carried by VOT, and that the cortical representation of both spectral and temporal cues in speech follows a common spatial coding scheme.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52, C59, C63, C82-C84 represent the main conclusions of the study. These conclusions are well-supported by the converging evidence from neural recordings (category selectivity, within-category encoding), classifier analyses (amplitude-based decoding), and computational modeling (mechanistic account). The tight stimulus control (C51) strengthens the conclusion that temporal cues are encoded spatially (C52). The claim of a unified coding scheme (C50, C59, C63, C84) is a major contribution supported by the data.

results.result: While temporal and amplitude codes for VOT are not mutually exclusive, with some electrodes showing temporal encoding in local field potentials, the amplitude of the peak high-gamma response emerged as a robust representation of voicing category, and the fact that cortical sites in every participant showed category-dependent amplitude differences rules out the possibility that these populations merely respond to spectral cues alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C58 address the relationship between temporal and amplitude coding. The exploratory LFP analyses (C53) show that temporal codes exist in some electrodes, but the main analyses (C54, C56) demonstrate that amplitude is the dominant code in high-gamma. The logical inference (C55) that category-dependent amplitude differences require temporal integration is sound. The acknowledgment of limitations (C57) is appropriate.

results.result: The computational model provides a parsimonious mechanistic account showing that gap and coincidence detection implemented through biologically-inspired microcircuits can naturally explain multiple patterns in the neural data, including category selectivity, asymmetric within-category encoding, and early temporal dynamics, without requiring specialized temporal codes.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62, C65-C66, C74 describe the explanatory power of the computational model. The model successfully captures multiple aspects of the neural data (C74) that were not explicitly designed into it (C65), including the asymmetric within-category encoding (C66). The conclusion that specialized temporal codes are not necessary (C62) is supported by the model's success. The model is appropriately described as parsimonious and biologically-inspired (C60).

results.result: Human nonprimary auditory cortex maintains a robust, graded representation of VOT that includes sub-phonetic details, and the same spatial/amplitude code that represents phonetic information can also accommodate sub-phonetic information, which is important because fine-grained acoustic detail has demonstrable effects on listeners' behavior and is necessary for perceptual learning and robust cue integration.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C70 connect the neural findings to behavioral significance. The graded representation (C67) is demonstrated by the within-category encoding results and supported by citations. The behavioral importance of sub-phonetic detail (C68-C69) is well-established in the literature with extensive citations. The conclusion that the spatial/amplitude code accommodates both phonetic and sub-phonetic information (C70) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Response onset latencies of V- electrodes were time-locked to the burst while V+ electrodes were time-locked to voicing onset, and the fact that the model's prediction of these onset latency dynamics is borne out in the neural data is consistent with local temporal integration in STG.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73 describe onset latency patterns and their implications. The time-locking patterns (C71-C72) are demonstrated in the data (Figure 3) and predicted by the model. The inference about local temporal integration (C73) is reasonable given the correspondence between model predictions and neural data, though the authors appropriately note that this doesn't definitively rule out integration at lower levels.

results.result: The model predicted VOT-dependence in the latency of the peak response in both Gap and Coinc units, but this fine-grained pattern was not found in the high-gamma data.
results.evaluation: Claim C75 describes a discrepancy between model predictions and neural data. The authors appropriately acknowledge this inconsistency and note uncertainty about whether it represents a false prediction or a signal-to-noise issue. This honest reporting of model limitations strengthens the overall credibility of the work.

results.result: VOT-sensitive neural populations were scattered throughout posterior and middle STG with no discernible topographical map of selectivity or evidence for lateralized asymmetries, with 76% located posterior to the transverse temporal sulcus and no significant differences in localization between V- and V+ electrodes or between hemispheres.
results.evaluation: Claims C76, C108-C111 describe the spatial distribution of VOT-sensitive sites. The statistical analyses (C109-C110) show no significant differences in localization (p=0.22, p=0.77 for spatial axes; p=0.70, p=0.19 for hemispheric differences). The conclusion of no topographical organization (C111) is appropriately qualified with acknowledgment of data limitations and is consistent with prior work on other phonetic features.

results.result: Exploratory analyses of auditory evoked local field potentials revealed complex associations between VOT and amplitude/temporal information carried in lower-frequency ranges.
results.evaluation: Claim C77 describes exploratory LFP findings shown in supplementary figures. While these analyses are less central to the main conclusions, they provide additional context about VOT encoding across different frequency ranges and are appropriately described as exploratory.

results.result: The present results are best interpreted as elucidating neural mechanisms of category perception, but not necessarily categorical perception, because acoustically distinct members of the same phonetic category are distinguishable in neural populations selective for that category, which would not be the case for truly categorical responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C80 provide an important conceptual clarification. The definition of truly categorical responses (C78) is supported by appropriate citations. The observation that within-category VOTs are distinguishable (C79) is demonstrated by the data. The interpretation (C80) appropriately distinguishes category perception from categorical perception, avoiding overclaiming about the nature of the neural representation.

results.result: The model suggests that top-down effects may not be a necessary condition for explaining the observed non-linear encoding patterns, though limited coverage beyond STG precludes ruling out top-down influences.
results.evaluation: Claim C81 appropriately acknowledges both the model's implications (that bottom-up mechanisms can explain the data) and the study's limitations (inability to rule out top-down effects due to limited coverage). This balanced interpretation is supported by citations to relevant theoretical work.

results.result: The findings add to a growing body of work highlighting the critical role of human STG as a sensory-perceptual computational hub in the speech perception system.
results.evaluation: Claim C85 places the findings in broader context and is supported by multiple citations to recent work on STG function. This represents an appropriate interpretation of the study's significance for understanding speech perception.

results.result: Seven participants with self-reported normal hearing were implanted with high-density ECoG arrays covering peri-Sylvian regions including STG as part of clinical treatment for epilepsy, with appropriate informed consent and ethical approval, and data from two additional participants were excluded due to excessive epileptiform activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C90 describe the participant population and ethical procedures. The methods are clearly described, ethical procedures are appropriate, and the exclusion criteria (C90) are reasonable. This represents standard methodology for ECoG studies in epilepsy patients.

results.result: Stimuli were generated using a Klatt synthesizer with all parameters held constant except the timing of voicing onset, which varied in 10 ms steps from 0 to 50 ms after burst onset, with all stimuli having a total duration of 300 ms and a 2 ms burst with constant spectral properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C94 describe the stimulus generation method in detail. The use of a Klatt synthesizer is standard for creating controlled speech stimuli, and the tight control of acoustic parameters (varying only VOT timing) is critical for isolating the temporal cue. The methods are clearly described and appropriate.

results.result: Four of seven participants performed a behavioral identification task indicating whether they heard 'ba' or 'pa' on each trial, with trials excluded if no response was made or reaction time exceeded three standard deviations from the mean, and behavioral data were analyzed using mixed effects logistic regression with VOT as a fixed effect and random intercepts for participants.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 describe the behavioral task and analysis methods. The task design is appropriate, exclusion criteria (C96) are reasonable, and the statistical analysis method (C97) is appropriate for binary response data with multiple participants. The mixed effects approach appropriately accounts for individual differences in category boundaries.

results.result: Neural data were recorded at ~3052 Hz, preprocessed with notch filtering and artifact rejection, and high-gamma activity (70-150 Hz) was extracted using the Hilbert transform and downsampled to 400 Hz. Speech-responsive electrodes (n=346) were identified based on anatomical location and elevated high-gamma activity, and VOT-sensitive electrodes (n=49) were identified using nonparametric correlation between VOT and peak high-gamma amplitude, with mean peak occurring 198.8 ms after stimulus onset.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C107 describe the neural data acquisition and preprocessing methods. The recording parameters are standard for ECoG, preprocessing steps are appropriate, the high-gamma extraction method follows established procedures (with citations), and the electrode selection criteria are clearly defined and statistically justified. The temporal resolution (400 Hz) is appropriate for detecting the 10 ms VOT differences.

results.result: A temporal cue that distinguishes speech sounds is represented by a spatial/amplitude code in human STG.
results.evaluation: Claim C36 is a summary statement of the main finding, supported by the converging evidence from neural recordings, classifier analyses, and computational modeling described in other results. This represents the core contribution of the study.

results.result: Recent ECoG evidence suggests that different neural populations also encode pitch and key properties of the speech envelope such as onsets and auditory edges.
results.evaluation: Claim C64 describes recent findings from other studies (supported by citations to Yi et al., 2019; Tang et al., 2017; Hamilton et al., 2018; Oganian and Chang, 2019) that provide context for the current work's contribution to understanding spatial coding in speech perception.
